subChunks.title: MVC Architecture

storyBeats.text: Eldrin redesigns the Academy's student management system. Before: one enormous class doing everything. After: three clean layers, each ignorant of the others' internals.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: MVC is separation of concerns made concrete. The Model owns the truth about your data. The View knows only how to display it. The Controller sits between them, directing traffic. Change the UI without touching the Model; change the database without touching the View.

storyBeats.label: MVC in action

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: In web frameworks like Spring MVC, the Controller is a class annotated @Controller, the Model is passed via Model parameter or DTOs, and the View is a template (Thymeleaf, etc.) or JSON response. The pattern scales to enterprise.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Implement a simple console MVC: Spell model (name, power), SpellView with display(String, int), and SpellController that updates and displays. Create a controller and call updateView().
guidedPractice.hint: SpellController holds both a Spell and SpellView. updateView() calls view.display(model.name, model.power).

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the three layers of MVC. What are the advantages of this separation?

questions.prompt: In MVC, which component is responsible for handling user input?
questions.explanation: The Controller receives user input, updates the Model, and tells the View to refresh. It mediates between input and output.

subChunks.title: Repository Pattern & Service Layer

storyBeats.text: Eldrin separates the Academy library into a public interface and a private filing system. The staff know the interface; only the librarian knows which physical room holds what.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The Repository pattern separates your business logic from data access. Your service talks to an interface — it doesn't know whether data lives in PostgreSQL, MongoDB, or a HashMap in memory. For tests, swap in the InMemory implementation. For production, plug in the real one.

storyBeats.label: Service + Repository

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: This is the power of programming to interfaces. Your SpellService could have been written and tested before the database implementation existed. The interface is the contract; implementations are interchangeable. Spring Data JPA generates the implementation automatically from the interface.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Implement: WizardRepository interface (save, findLevel returning Optional<Integer>), InMemoryWizardRepository, and WizardService that uses it. Register 'Merlin' and retrieve their info.
guidedPractice.hint: InMemoryWizardRepository uses a HashMap<String, Integer>. findLevel returns Optional.ofNullable(store.get(name)).

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: What are the benefits of the Repository pattern? How does it improve testability?

questions.prompt: Your service class directly uses new JdbcWizardRepository() inside its methods. What problem does this create?
options: Tight coupling — you cannot swap the repository for testing or changing databases
It is slower than using an interface
questions.answer: Tight coupling — you cannot swap the repository for testing or changing databases
questions.explanation: Using new inside a service creates a hard dependency on the specific implementation. You cannot swap an in-memory repository for tests without modifying the service. Inject the interface via constructor instead.

subChunks.title: SOLID Principles

storyBeats.text: Eldrin stands before a wall etched with five runes — the SOLID principles. 'These are not rules to memorise,' he says, 'they are questions to ask of every class you write.'

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Does this class have one reason to change? Can I extend it without modifying it? If I replace it with a subclass, will things still work? Am I forcing clients to depend on methods they don't need? Am I depending on abstractions or concrete details?

storyBeats.label: SRP and OCP

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: These principles do not guarantee good code — but violating them consistently guarantees fragile, tightly-coupled code that is painful to test and terrifying to change. Apply them as lenses, not as dogma.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Demonstrate Dependency Inversion: create an interface Logger with log(String msg). Implement ConsoleLogger and SilentLogger. Create SpellCaster that accepts a Logger via constructor and logs before casting. Demonstrate both loggers.
guidedPractice.hint: SpellCaster depends on Logger (interface), not ConsoleLogger (concrete). This is DIP in action.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the Dependency Inversion Principle. How does constructor injection relate to it?

questions.prompt: Which SOLID principle says a class should have only one reason to change?
questions.explanation: SRP: a class should have exactly one reason to change — meaning it should encapsulate one cohesive responsibility. If two concerns change for different reasons, split them into separate classes.

questions.prompt: You have a ReportService class that: fetches data from a database, formats it as HTML, and sends it via email. A new requirement arrives: support PDF format and also send via Slack. Which SOLID principle is being violated and what should you do?
options: Single Responsibility (and Open/Closed) — split into DataFetcher, ReportFormatter (interface + HTMLFormatter/PDFFormatter), and NotificationSender (interface + EmailSender/SlackSender)
Liskov Substitution — use a base class for all formats
Interface Segregation — merge all methods into one interface
Dependency Inversion — use static utility methods
questions.answer: Single Responsibility (and Open/Closed) — split into DataFetcher, ReportFormatter (interface + HTMLFormatter/PDFFormatter), and NotificationSender (interface + EmailSender/SlackSender)
questions.explanation: The class has three responsibilities, each with its own reason to change. Applying SRP produces three separate concerns; applying OCP with interfaces for formatting and sending makes the system extensible without modifying existing classes.
